newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian leaders seek to balance racism, politics.
newsitem.headline: Australian leaders seek to balance racism, politics.

text.p: Australia's political leaders are walking a dangerous path between condemning racial bigots and pandering to popular racist feeling amid a renewed row over race and immigration, analysts said on Sunday.
Racism and racial issues have begun dominating public debate and are expected to figure heavily in a critical by-election next Saturday.
Opinion polls show strong anti-Asian and anti-immigration sentiment, against a background of increasing reports of a sometimes violent backlash against Asian immigrants and tourists.
"People pick up the message and start behaving in different ways," political scientist Jim Jupp told Reuters.
"Hoons (hooligans) get the message that it's alright to go out and be a bit nasty," said Jupp, director of the Australian National University's centre for immigration and multicultural studies.

But Jupp said neither the conservative Liberal-National government nor the Labor opposition wanted to risk alienating a substantial number of voters by coming out too strongly against recent racist comments by some politicians.
"I don't think either side is going to stand up and take a position now, because it's all a bit dodgy," he said. "They don't know what's going on in the mind of the community."
Opposition leader Kim Beazley made his strongest statement on the issue during a prepared speech to ethnic broadcasters on Friday, saying multiculturalism had enriched Australia.
"I don't know how you can abolish multiculturalism," Beazley said.

"You might as well call for the abolition of mateship for all the impact you can have on something which has been such a success and such a defining aspect of the building of the modern Australian nation."
Australia's race debate was reignited a month ago by a disgraced former member of Prime Minister John Howard's Liberal Party, Pauline Hanson, now in parliament as an independent.
Hanson, a fish-and-chip shop owner from the socially and politically conservative Queensland state, said in her first speech to parliament that Asians were "swamping" Australia.
Asians make up about a quarter of the approximately 100,000 immigrants who arrive in Australia,

Hanson also said Asian countries posed a military threat, and has made a series of anti-Aboriginal comments. Howard, while rejecting racism itself, has refused in parliament to repudiate Hanson's comments.
Hanson was dumped from the Liberal Party for similar controversial remarks earlier this year.
An opinion poll published in last Tuesday's The Sydney Morning Herald newspaper found 48 percent of respondents backed Hanson, while only 38 percent disagreed.
Political commentator Alan Ramsey said Howard and Beazley had carefully avoided being drawn into the uproar sparked by Hanson's comments.
"And that, of course, is what this whole grubby business has been about: political self-interest," Ramsay wrote in Wednesday's Herald.
"Pauline Hanson's speech struck a deep chord in the electorate that neither John Howard nor Kim Beazley is anxious to offend or alienate."
A Canberra-based Asian official and Jupp said the October 19 by-election for a government-held Sydney seat would be an important indication of whether the race row would continue.
Australia's anti-immigration party on Wednesday launched its campaign for the seat, blaming immigrants for high unemployment, and health problems such as hepatitis B and tuberculosis.

"Australia went to great lengths to eradicate tuberculosis and yet in an area of Melbourne with a high Asian population there has been this remarkable outbreak with 150 nurses testing positive," independent parliamentarian Graeme Campbell told the Australians Against Further Immigrgation campaign launch.
Campbell was dumped from the Labor Party in 1995 for his controversial anti-Asian and anti-immigration comments.
